newsitem.title: USA: Publix grocery chain sued for race discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Publix grocery chain sued for race discrimination.

text.p: Publix Super Markets Inc. was sued in federal court Thursday by a group of black workers who alleged the grocery chain discriminated against them, 10 weeks after Publix settled a discrimination lawsuit by female employees.

The United Food and Commercial Workers Union, or UFCW, announced at a news conference that some of its members had filed suit in U.S. District Court alleging the Lakeland, Fla.-based company systematically discriminated against minority workers.
The union, which said it had no direct involvement in the lawsuit, said Publix refused to hire or promote black workers and created a workplace "littered with racial slurs and hostility."
Publix spokeswoman Jennifer Bush called the lawsuit "yet another UFCW publicity stunt," adding that the number of black managers at Publix had tripled since 1990.
"Harassment of any kind is an intolerable violation of company policy," she said. "When we learn of such incidents, we investigate and take appropriate action, which can include termination."
Privately held Publix, the nation's eighth-largest supermarket chain with 540 stores in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina and Alabama, employs more than 100,000 workers.

Sixteen Publix workers were named as plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which was filed as a class action on behalf of about 9,000 black Publix employees, lawyers said. The union said the class could expand to cover about 20,000 when former employees or people denied jobs were added.
The lawsuit did not name a specific damage figure.
The lawsuit alleged various forms of racial discrimination, including the coding of employment applications according to race.

The union encouraged a similar class action in 1996, claiming women were systematically denied management opportunities at Publix. The company settled in January, admitting no responsibility but agreeing to pay out $81.5 million to women employed at Publix as long ago as May 1991.
UFCW Southeast Regional Director Willie Baker Jr. said he expected the race discrimination lawsuit to cost Publix more than the settlement in the sex discrimination case.
At the news conference, the union presented four former Publix workers who were not among the named plaintiffs but alleged discrimination by Publix.
"When I asked for promotion to a management job, the manager laughed in my face," said Joan Robinson, who said she worked as a Publix bagger for two years.

Publix said in a statement it had more than 400 blacks in management positions, representing nearly 6 percent of its managers. "The company expects that percentage to continue its upward trend," the statement said.
The union countered by saying that Publix reclassifies positions to make them appear to be management without actually increasing responsibilities or pay.
